Welcome to Bronte School
Bronte School is an independent preparatory school for 3 to 11 year olds. Its setting is a fine, spacious building, with plenty of outdoor garden and play areas, in the centre of Gravesend, 3 or 4 minutes from the station.
Bronte School is academically selective, yet maintains a strong family feel. It is conveniently located in the centre of Gravesend with fast commuter links to London, ideal for families living in Istead Rise, Meopham, Cobham, Shorne, Longfield or the Ebbsfleet and Dartford area.
About Bronte School
All we offer here at Bronte School is a source of great pride for me and for my colleagues: a very special combination of academic rigour and a family-orientated, personal approach.
Emma WoodHeadmistress, Bronte School
Most pupils go on to achieve places in highly selective secondary schools. Pupils' academic outcomes are a significant strength of the school.
Our School
Watch our video below to get an insight into Bronte School
Nurture your child's growth
See firsthand how we help your child uncover their unique talents and passions through the endless opportunities at Bronte School.

Inspection Report 2025
The full report is available here.
Bronte School was found by inspectors to be fully compliant in all areas of school life, and pupils’ academic outcomes were recognised as a significant strength of the School.
This is a rare and prestigious accolade: an area of significant strength is considered noteworthy because only a very small proportion of schools inspected are awarded such recognition.
As of July 2025, only 10% of independent schools inspected by ISI have received this distinction in their reports.
Over the course of four days, a rigorous and thorough review of every aspect of the School was conducted by the inspection team. Under the new ISI framework, overall grades or judgements are no longer given; instead, inspectors highlight areas where exceptional practice is observed to have a profound and genuine impact on pupils’ development — and it was made clear that the academic achievement and wellbeing of pupils at Bronte School were regarded as truly exceptional.
The report notes that the School’s teaching, curriculum and learning environment enable pupils to develop a love of learning, achieve highly, and leave Bronte exceptionally well prepared for the next stage of their education.
This recognition reflects the dedication of staff, the commitment of pupils, and the invaluable support of the parent community.
This outcome is a source of great pride to the School, and parents are warmly encouraged to read the full report in order to appreciate the many strengths that have been celebrated.
Below, a few of the key findings from the report have been highlighted:
A culture of kindness pervades the school.

Fees and Charges 2026 -2027
Fees and Charges 2026 – 2027
Our school fees are charged a term in advance and reviewed annually.
School Fee Plan provides parents the opportunity to pay via a monthly direct debit over 12 months. If you would like more information, please contact the Bursar.
We offer a Fees in Advance scheme, please click here for more information or alternatively please contact the Bursar. Please note, the School will continue to review fees on an annual basis and pass on any increases to advance fee payers. Therefore fees will not be ‘fixed’ by paying in advance.
In-house 10-month payment plan
Parents wishing to choose this option should contact the Bursar by July 31st so arrangements can be made.
Childcare Voucher Scheme
The school accepts voucher payments for childcare from most voucher companies, including vouchers from the Government Childcare Tax-free Voucher Scheme. Information on the scheme, and to register, can be found on the GOV.UK website.
Childcare vouchers are also available through many companies as a method of obtaining vouchers with minimal tax commitment. If your company participates in such a scheme, salary deductions can be applied each month, which will not thereby be subject to Income Tax or National Insurance. Your company will then pass on the full amount to its associated voucher company.
Fees are payable with cleared funds by noon on the first day of each term. In the event of late payment, an administrative surcharge of £100 is applicable. Interest, at an annual rate of base rate plus 7.5%, is payable on any debt outstanding after 30 days.

An additional fee is charged for dedicated, formally arranged, one-to-one classroom learning support. The hours charged incorporate provision for assessment and observations, individualised planning and parent meetings, as well as actual one-to-one support with the child. This support may include provision based on recommendations from an outside agency. Charging is termly, and depends on the number of learning support hours provided. As an example, the fee for provision of 2 hours learning support per day, for 5 days per week, a total of 10 hours per week, is £3,200 per term. The fee for other amounts of provision is worked out on a pro rata basis: thus the charge for 2 hours per week would be £640 per term. If parents are seeking to apply to the local authority for an education, health and care (EHC) plan, the School will be required to complete the necessary formal assessments and other preparatory tasks. A charge of £580.00 is made for this work.
Should parents wish to withdraw a child prior to the end of Year 6, a full term’s notice is required. Details are given in the Parent-School Agreement.
Individual Illness or Absence
If, for an extended period, a child has to be away from the School because of illness or because of family circumstances, such as a defined temporary period spent away from the area, fees remain payable as normal. If the period of absence extends to more than one term, the School will liaise with parents concerning the individual situation, and fees payable will be discussed.
From the start of such absence, the School will seek to provide, within practical and reasonable limitations, on-going educational support for the child. This could include regular teacher contact, and general support, for example through some remote learning provision. The nature and level of such support will inevitably depend on the individual situation.
Temporary School Closure
If the School has to close temporarily because of adverse weather, damage and subsequent repairs to the property, or any other event or circumstance affecting safety or the School’s ability to operate, fees remain payable as normal. If the period of closure extends to more than one term, the School will consider the situation and the level of fees payable.
From the start of such closure, the School will seek to provide, within practical and reasonable limitations, on-going educational support for all children. It is anticipated that, assuming it is possible to do so, “Bronte Remote Learning” provision would be initiated at as early a stage as possible.
1. General. Lessons are available in guitar, piano and violin. As well as the lessons themselves, there are performance opportunities at concerts and other school events, annual reports and guidance for Associated Board Examinations.
2. Timings. Lessons take place during the school day, either during a break or during an academic lesson. Every effort is made to ensure that a same subject and lesson time is not used each week. Ensembles take place at lunchtime or after school.
3. Ensembles. Participation in an ensemble, such as the Rock Band or Guitar Group, is subject to vacancy and also requires a minimum standard. Further details are given on the “Clubs and Activities” choices form sent out at the end of each term, for bookings for the term ahead.
4. Missed Lessons. If a pupil misses a lesson for any reason, the teacher will attempt to make up the lesson at another time during the term or school year. If the pupil misses a lesson because of a school trip, the lesson will be made up at another time during the term or school year. Normally lessons are not timetabled when there is a known absence arising from a school trip or event.
5. Notice to Cease Lessons or Ensembles. Half a term’s notice is required. If this notice is not given, a half term’s fees are payable.

Headmistress’s Welcome
All we offer here at Bronte School is a source of great pride for me and for my colleagues: a very special combination of academic rigour and a family-orientated, personal approach.
We emphasise good learning, enquiry and discovery in all areas: English and mathematics (the core subjects), humanities, languages, music, the performing and visual arts, science and sport. In pastoral care, we get to know and nurture each individual boy and girl, to ensure that talents and interests are fostered, and achievements celebrated.
In my own life, as mother to three children, I witnessed at first-hand how early experiences shaped whole futures, something which helped create my passion for young children’s education. Since joining Bronte, I have seen successive generations of children entering the School at age 3 or 4, some of whom may perhaps be a little nervous or shy, and leaving aged 11 as confident, articulate and successful young people. Witnessing such paths of happy growth gives everyone here tremendous satisfaction and joy.
Good education is a high ideal, and I believe in the idea of education being expansive and big-minded, bringing to young people assurance and adaptability for the adult world. A fundamental part of Bronte’s life and mission is to play its part in that great journey, by preparing children for their senior schools. We have been delighted with successes achieved. Many of our pupils go to highly selective grammar schools, for example, or to leading independent schools, often with scholarships. The most important aim, even so, is always to find the right school for each individual, where he or she will flourish and flower.
All this can be summed up by saying that at Bronte, we seek for each boy or girl to grow into the best and most fulfilling version of themselves.
Emma Wood Headmistress, Bronte School
"An ambitious, well-planned and well-resourced curriculum, highly effective teaching, meticulous assessment tracking and timely support for pupils result in an exceptionally high-quality outcome."

Nature, Ethos & Aims
Bronte School is an independent, co-educational day preparatory school, for children ages 3 to 11. The School seeks to provide high quality education, within a balanced curriculum, which nurtures development and provides the challenges needed for growth. The twin pillars of being a family school and of upholding excellence in academic life are at the heart of the school’s ethos.
The School has a Christian character and tradition, and welcomes families and staff from any background, ethnicity or religion. All within the School community are encouraged to strive to treat others as they would wish to be treated themselves.
A culture of kindness pervades the school.

Parents' Council
Acting as a channel for parental suggestions and opinion, the Parents’ Council meets once per term.
There are between 6 and 8 parent members, each representing one or two year groups.
The willingness of parents to give their time for the Council is much appreciated.
School Representatives
Any parent always has direct access to the Headmistress or any staff member. However, some parents find the Council a helpful route to share a point or enquiry.
You can contact any Council member, though you would normally approach the representative for your child’s year group.
If you volunteer in one year and a place isn’t available, it is often possible, given the normal turn-around in membership, that your offer can be taken up in a following year.
For queries or to express interest in joining, please contact the School Office or your year group representative.
Meets once per term.
Chair: Headmistress
Members: Deputy Head, Registrar/Office Manager
Open to any current parent.

Bronte Nursery
Bronte Nursery is Bronte School’s sister setting, providing 51 weeks per year of high quality care for children from 3 months to 5 years old. Located just along Pelham Road from the school, the Nursery is conveniently situated both for the School and for Gravesend train station.
The aim of the Nursery is to provide a caring, family feel, where opportunities for play abound and where there is always the reassuring and familiar presence of staff. In parallel, breadth and strong educational foundations are introduced progressively at the different ages, with French, ballet, music and PE included as part of the weekly programmes.
The setting is a substantial, traditional house, with plenty of space, in the rooms and in the garden. The hall is an alternative space for indoor games, teaching and activities, as well as where older children eat their meals. There is short term parking available at the front of the Nursery. The building has recently been extended and refurbished, to create a lovely new feel and excellent new facilities.

pageCache.pageTitle: Entry into Later Years - Bronte School
pageCache.text:
Entry into Later Years
Most children join Bronte School in their Kindergarten year, when the majority of places are offered. However, from time to time, spaces do become available in Reception or other year groups. As an academically selective school, any place can only be offered following a successful Assessment and Familiarisation Day, during which we get to know your child and ensure that Bronte School is the right fit for them.
To enquire about current availability or to begin the admissions process, please contact our Registrar, Nicky Mason ([email protected]), who will be happy to guide you through the next steps.

History
The founder of Bronte School, in 1905, was Mrs Katherine Vine (née Palmer). Born in 1864, Mrs Vine is recorded in the 1881 Census as a Miss Palmer, aged 17, a ‘scholar’. She founded the School in the large house on Parrock Street, 6, Bronte Villas, which was presumably also the Vines’ family home. It is assumed that she was in charge of the School right from its start. Certainly, in the 1911 census, when she was 47, she is listed as a ‘school principal’.
Catherine’s husband, William Vine, was a shipping merchant, and one imagines that he could have had riverside offices in Gravesend. He must presumably have been sympathetic with his wife’s desire to start a school, not least as Bronte must have occupied much of his house. Perhaps also, assuming his business was doing well, he provided financial support, at the foundation, and maybe subsequently too.
It is worth reflecting upon the origins of the name ‘Bronte’. One idea which has been put forward is that a family including three sisters and a brother, was somehow associated with the famous Bronte family of Charlotte, Emily, Ann and their brother Banwell. (two other Bronte sisters, Maria and Elizabeth, died in childhood). However, Jane Eyre, Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey, the novels which propelled the three authors to fame, were not published until 1847, 15 years after the building of Bronte Villas in 1832. This theory thus seems very unlikely.
A much more likely explanation would seem to be that the school was simply named after its own premises, Bronte Villas.
The likely origin of that name provides a link for the school with Admiral Lord Nelson. One of his titles was Duke of Bronte (a village in Sicily), conferred on him in 1799 by the King of Naples, in gratitude for assistance in relieving the French naval blockade of the city. Given that Bronte Villas was built in distinct living memory of the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805, it seems very plausible that the terrace was named in honour of Nelson.
There is another story about the name ‘Bronte’, which curiously brings the Bronte sisters back into the picture. The original surname of the sisters’ father, Patrick (1771 – 1861), was ‘Brunty’. At some point he changed the spelling to Bronte. One theory (there are others) for this slightly eccentric thing to have done is that he had a desire to have an association with Lord Nelson, Duke of Bronte. Whatever else can be deduced about all this, it does seem that Nelson’s Bronte title was very well known, and this in turn lends weight to the idea that Bronte Villas, set on higher ground overlooking the lower Thames, was indeed named in honour of Nelson.
Katherine Vine might well have had Nelson in mind too, when she named her school. This does not seem unlikely, the school being founded in the centenary year of Nelson’s famous victory at Trafalgar.
It is not known when Bronte’s two pupil houses, Nelson and Hood, were named, but the names underpin the idea of a School having some historic naval links, and also reflect the strong maritime tradition of Gravesend itself. Vice-Admiral Horatio Nelson, 1st Viscount Nelson and 1st Duke of Bronte, KB, (1758 – 1805) needs no introduction of course. Vice-Admiral Alexander Hood, 1st Viscount Bridport, KB, (1726 – 1814) was a contemporary of Nelson, his life of 88 years spanning Nelson’s 47 years. He had a highly distinguished naval career, serving in the Seven Years’ War (1756 – 83), the American War of Independence and the French Revolutionary Wars (1792 -1802). He retired from the Royal Navy in 1800. His career also included two spells as a Member of Parliament. He was Member for Bridgwater (1784 – 90) and for Buckingham (1790 – 96).
Turning back to the School’s early years, Katherine and William had three daughters, Florence (b. 1894), Alice (also known as Ivy) (b. 1900) and Enid (b. 1904), and a son, Christopher (b. 1896). Tragically, Christopher was killed in World War 1, aged 20, in August 1916. Thus it was that the Vines became one more of the countless thousands upon thousands of families who had to endure grievous loss and bereavement.
Each of the girls was involved with teaching at Bronte, Florence and Alice also being musicians. Their mother Katherine died in 1932, aged 68, and the ownership and running of Bronte School passed to the three daughters.
Relatively little is known about Florence: in 1927, she is recorded as a ‘school and music mistress’. As far as we can tell, she, Alice (‘school mistress and organist’) and Enid (‘pupil teacher’) jointly owned the school for all their respective lives. Enid died in 1977 and Alice in 1975. None of the sisters married: so many men had been lost of course that many young women found themselves in this situation. Yet it is surely the case that the three sisters faithfully devoted themselves wholly and fully to the care and teaching of the children at Bronte. It cannot have been at all easy keeping going during the national economic difficulties of the 1930s, though the years of war from 1939 to 1945, and then through the deprivations of the 1950s. Yet keep going they assuredly did. At the time of Alice’s death, Bronte had been owned and cared for by the Vine family for a remarkable 72 years.
Even so, notwithstanding the sisters’ dedicated, vocational commitment, the School found itself, in the early and mid 1970s, facing something of a crisis, with reduced pupil numbers and attendant financial pressures. There was a strong core, however, of loyal, appreciative families who valued the School’s traditions. One such family, Peers and Susan Carter and their three daughters, resolved to acquire Bronte and build it up again This they did, and over the following decades the School grew and flourished, a tribute to the investment and commitment of the Carters and to the leadership and dedication of successive Heads and staff. The Carters also founded Bronte Nursery, having purchased suitable premises, 21, Pelham Road, about 200 yards from the School.
After no less than 36 years as owners, the Carters were approaching retirement, as was Richard Dyson, who had been the School’s, very successful Headmaster, since 2003. New ownership was sought. A new proprietor and headmaster, Nicholas Clements, took over Bronte in 2014, following a career and headship in senior education. At this time the Advisory Board was also established, to support the governance of the School and the Nursery, its membership currently comprising Margie Dyson, Charles LeBrun, Robin Lewis and Catherine Mentzel (see their bios).
In April 2017, Emma Wood moved from her role as Deputy Head to become Headmistress of Bronte School and Director of Bronte Nursery. Nicholas Clements remained as Proprietor until June 2025 when he sadly passed away, and his wife Fenella Clements took on this role.
The life of Bronte, started in 1905, happily and successfully thrives, and long may it continue to do so.

Kindergarten
The Kindergarten class is for the pre-school year (ages 3 and 4). Most children join Bronte School in this year. The class provides a happy, secure foundation for school life and the transition to the Reception year.
Kindergarten has a very gentle feel, akin to a Nursery, with a slightly more school-type atmosphere and routine. Children attending Kindergarten start with a minimum of three full days, increasing to a minimum of four days in the Spring Term.
Building upon the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) framework, the Kindergarten curriculum employs a variety of approaches: staff-led guidance and teaching is mixed with wide opportunities for play, in order that day-by-day the children can contentedly grow, enjoy and learn for themselves.
There are, too, group activities designed to promote healthy and strong growth and the building of skills. Dough Gym, Funky Fingers and Write Dance, for example, mix fun and a focussed development of the muscle control skills needed when progressing to writing.
Creativity and breadth of experience is enhanced by music, choir, art and PE and Forest School sessions, and by full involvement in school events such as French Day, special assemblies, service visits and charity days.
"Children in the early years thrive due to the high standards of care they receive from staff. The curriculum is skilfully adapted to nurture children's interests and support their development and learning."

Selection Test Results
"Pupils develop a love of learning and enthusiastically engage in regular challenges to apply what they have learnt in increasingly complex and independent ways. Most pupils go on to achieve places in highly selective secondary schools. Pupils' academic outcomes are a significant strength of the school."

Structure, Governance, Advisory Board
Bronte is an independent school for children aged 3 to 11, registered with and inspected by the Independent Schools Inspectorate (ISI). ISI reports to the Department for Education, and regulates almost all independent schools.
Bronte School is privately-owned, and the Proprietor is Fenella Clements, who is also Proprietor of Bronte Nursery.
In defined responsibilities, the Proprietor is responsible for the governance of the School, and thereby for safety, welfare and overall educational development, as well as for finance and general strategy.
The Headmistress of the School, Emma Wood (who is also Director of the Nursery) leads the School, and is thereby responsible for the education of the children, for the management, safety and welfare of all in the School community, and for the School’s strategic development and vision. As headmistress, she is a member of the Independent Schools Association (ISA), which is part of the Independent Schools Council (ISC).
The Bursar of Bronte School and Nursery, Siobhan Bradish, is responsible for financial management and for HR management. She is the manager of the Support Staff, and is responsible for the environment and for building maintenance.
The Bronte School and Nursery Advisory Board supports the governance of the School and of the Nursery. Advisory Board members visit at least twice a year, meeting staff and children, observing aspects of school life and receiving reports and briefings.
During school closure the Proprietor, Fenella Clements, at 7 Pelham Road, Gravesend, Kent, DA11 0HN can be contacted by telephone at 01474 533705.
Fenella ClementsProprietor
Following a degree in English at Exeter University, Fenella went on to train as a lawyer and practised as a solicitor for two and a half years in London. She then decided to pursue her lifelong love of music at Trinity College of Music, gaining a Postgraduate Certificate and a ‘cello teaching Diploma. Whilst there she discovered the joy of teaching, and has since taught ‘cello, piano and violin both privately and as a peripatetic teacher in various schools in London, Somerset, Yorkshire and Kent. She has performed too in a range of settings including theatres, weddings, private events and orchestras.
Since being married to Nicholas (1996) there have also been various roles to fill within the schools where he was headmaster, and with him she has brought up their three children, Lucinda, Oliver, and Dominic. Since 2014 she has had the pleasure and joy of getting to know Bronte alongside him as he held the positions of headmaster and proprietor.
Now as sole proprietor in his stead, she will continue to promote his vision of the ethos and aims of Bronte.
Margie DysonAdvisory Board
Margie began her nursing career at St. George’s Hospital in London. She then served as a school nurse in the Borough of Haringey and at a school for children with additional needs.
Margie subsequently worked in the three schools where her husband, Richard, was Headmaster: Wellingborough Junior School, St. Faith’s School, Cambridge, and Bronte School. With over four decades of experience living and working in schools, she brings a wealth of knowledge and care to the Advisory Board.
Margie has three children and four grandchildren and lives in Cambridge.
Colonel Charles Le BrunAdvisory Board
Charles Le Brun was born in Beverley, East Yorkshire and was educated at Pocklington School, York, The Royal Military Academy, Sandhurst and the Army Staff College, Camberley. He had a full career in the British Army as an infantry officer in The Prince of Wales’s Own Regiment of Yorkshire and latterly in The Royal Yorkshire Regiment. Thereafter he was 9 years in the Armed Forces of The United Arab Emirates as a military trainer and advisor.During his time in the British Army he served in Great Britain, Northern Ireland, Germany, Norway, Kuwait and Jamaica, where he was the defence adviser in the British High Commission, from there he covered the Bahamas, The Turks and Caicos Islands and the Western Caribbean. Whilst in Kuwait he chaired the governing committee of The English School – the country’s oldest international school, which three of his four children then attended.
Charles now lives in East Yorkshire and remains closely engaged with his old regiments, as chairman of The Prince of Wales’s Own regimental association and as the heritage trustee for the Royal Yorkshire Regiment. He enjoys history, current affairs, 18th and 19th Century architecture and furniture and restoring his early Victorian house.
Robin LewisAdvisory Board
Educated at Bedford Modern School and the Universities of Nottingham, Loughborough and Cambridge [Wolfson College visiting scholar], Robin spent 20 years teaching Biology and PE at an HMC school in the West Country, 13 of those years as a boarding housemaster. He then enjoyed 9 years leading two independent boarding preparatory schools and becoming an inspector. In 1998 the English Speaking Union awarded him a prestigious Walter Hines Page travelling scholarship to the United States. In 2000, as a result of his wife’s serious illness, he resigned his headship and returned to teaching taking fixed term contracts at a wide variety of schools and increasing his consultative and inspectorial experience. He was made a Reporting [Lead] Inspector with the Independent Schools’ Inspectorate in 2008 and runs his own consultancy.
Catherine MentzelAdvisory Board
Catherine Mentzel trained at King’s College London and worked as a Trauma and Intensive Care Unit nurse, a career which has proved to be a great grounding for coping in later life with the joys and dramas of being a mother and army wife! She is married to Kevin, an Army chaplain, and they have two daughters at an independent school in Oxfordshire.
Catherine enjoys seeing everyday school life and has served as a Foundation Governor, chaired the Curriculum and Standards committee and was involved with the appointment of a new Headteacher at a primary school in Hampshire. Other duties have involved running childrens’ music groups, a school gardening club, and even a spell as a “dinner lady”. She lives near Oxford and works part time at a local prep school.

Admission Process
The best way to find out about Bronte is to visit and see the School for yourself. A visit and tour can be arranged at any time during term-time and will include a meeting with the Headmistress or Deputy Head, as well as the opportunity to meet your child’s prospective class teacher.
To arrange a visit, please contact Nicky Mason, Registrar, on 01474 533805 or e-mail [email protected].
We look forward to welcoming you.
Admissions Procedure
Following an enquiry or visit, you may wish to register. This involves submission of a form, together with the non-refundable registration fee (£120) and original birth certificate or passport. Registration ensures that we stay in touch, and enables an “Assessment and Familiarisation Visit” (AFV) to take place.
The AFV is important for both the family and the school. It allows observation of a child in the School setting, as well as allowing the child and parents to get a further feel for the School and to affirm that the environment suits. School or nursery reports are usually also requested at this stage.
Shortly after the AFV, the School will contact you to confirm whether a place can be offered.
Most children join Bronte in the Kindergarten class (for children aged 3 on 1st September of the year of entry). Early application is advisable.
Places do occasionally arise in Reception class and other classes: do enquire about entry with the Registrar ([email protected]).

Holiday Activities
Summer and Easter Camps
Over the Summer and Easter breaks, it can be a daunting task to find good quality childcare where the children can be well looked after and happily play together. Bronte Camps operate for one week during the Easter holidays and for the first three weeks of the summer holidays. Bronte children can relax and have fun in a safe environment, with familiar members of staff.
Camp days comprise activities and games organised by staff, and plenty of non-structured time when the children play by themselves — usually outside, but sometimes inside if the weather is poor.
Immediately after the end of the Autumn Term, there is a Christmas Club, normally held over two days. This is filled with festive craft activities, including present-wrapping skills, a Christmas party, and lots of fun and games. The Club also gives parents a chance for some secret present-buying and wrapping!
Year 5 Revision Course
For children about to move into Year 6 there is a Revision Course held during the last full week of the summer holidays. The course is either 4 or 5 days long (Monday is sometimes a bank holiday).

Minibuses and Transport
The School provides early morning pick-up and afternoon drop-off services for pupils who need transport to and from school. The service is “hand-to-hand”, children being taken to and from their home or a designated pick-up point, and transferred personally to and from their parents or childminders/carers.
The drivers are employed directly by the school, and they soon get to know the children well too, and quickly become familiar with the various needs and with inevitable changes to requirements. All drivers of course are given full Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) checks.
CCTV cameras are fitted in both vehicles and record live action whilst the minibuses are being used, both within the vehicle and on the road. This provides protection and information in the event of an accident or incident and is standard practice in commercial vehicles.
Our school minibus serves the areas of Gravesend, Greenhithe and Dartford. Morning collection usually begins around 7.30am, with arrival at the school expected by 8.30am. For the afternoon service pupils are escorted to the minibus by their teachers at 3.30pm. Expected arrival time will be advised at the beginning of each term, once a place on the minibus has been confirmed.
Bookings are preferred termly in advance although ad-hoc journeys may be possible if spare capacity is available. Please contact the office on 01474 533805 to confirm if capacity available for ad-hoc journeys.
Places are booked termly using a booking sheet issued to all parents towards the end of each term, for the following term.
